Chapter 8: The World as a Limited Whole—What Lies Beyond.
So, after looking at the boundaries of language, logic, and even the self, let's turn our attention to something big—the world as a whole.
If we think about it, the world is really just the sum total of all the facts we can describe or imagine. But do you ever get that feeling—maybe when you're standing under a vast night sky, or pausing for a moment of deep reflection—that there's something more? Something just beyond what you can put into words?
That sense of “something more” is actually pretty common. It's that moment of awe or wonder, when you feel like the world, for all its detail and richness, might not be the whole story.
But here's where it gets fascinating. According to the way we've been looking at things, anything that’s beyond the world of facts can’t really be pictured or described in language. It's unsayable—literally outside the reach of words.
Let's break down the key points:
First, the world is made up of facts—everything we can describe or imagine is inside that boundary.
Second, when we feel there's “something more,” we're touching on what lies beyond both language and facts.
Third, whatever is beyond that boundary? It can’t be directly said or described. It’s simply out of reach for language.
And finally, this isn’t a problem with our way of thinking. In fact, it's how meaning works. The boundary isn’t a flaw—it’s part of the beauty.
Recognizing this can feel both humbling and surprisingly freeing.
It invites us to really appreciate the world as it is—knowing that some mysteries will always remain out there, just beyond our grasp.
The edge of the world isn’t a wall to crash through. It’s more like a horizon we can see, but never quite reach.
In this light, the limits of language aren’t something to get frustrated about. They can actually become a source of wonder—reminding us that, sometimes, the most meaningful things are the ones we can't quite say.
